title: Chapter 26
paragraphs: In the morning Konstantin Levin left Moscow, and toward evening he reached home. On the train journey he talked to his neighbors about politics and the new railways, and just as in Moscow he was overcome by a confusion of ideas, dissatisfaction with himself, shame about something or other. But when he got out at his own station, when he saw his one-eyed coachman Ignat with the collar of his coat turned up; when, in the dim light reflected by the station fires, he saw his own sledge, his own horses with their tails tied up, in their harness trimmed with rings and tassels; when the coachman Ignat, as he was loading the luggage, told him the village news — that the contractor had arrived, and that Pava had calved — he felt the confusion gradually clearing up, and the shame and self-dissatisfaction passing away. He felt this at the mere sight of Ignat and the horses; but when he had put on the sheepskin coat brought for him, had settled himself wrapped up in the sledge and driven off, pondering the work ahead of him in the village and watching the side-horse that had once been his saddle-horse, past its prime now but still a spirited beast from the Don, he began to see what had happened to him in a quite different light. He felt himself, and did not want to be anyone else. All he wanted now was to be better than he had been. In the first place he resolved that from that day on he would give up hoping for the kind of extraordinary happiness marriage was supposed to bring him, and consequently would no longer disdain what he really had. Secondly, he would never again let himself give way to low passion, the memory of which had so tortured him while he was making up his mind to propose. Then, remembering his brother Nikolay, he resolved that he would never allow himself to forget him, that he would keep an eye on him and not lose track of him, so as to be ready to help when things took a bad turn. And that would be soon, he felt. Then, too, his brother's talk of communism, which he had treated so lightly at the time, now made him think. He considered a revolution in economic conditions nonsense. But he had always felt the injustice of his own abundance compared with the poverty of the peasants, and now he resolved that, to feel quite in the right — though he had worked hard and lived no luxurious life before — he would now work still harder and allow himself even less luxury. And all this seemed to him so easy a conquest over himself that he spent the whole drive in the pleasantest daydreams. With a firm sense of hope in a new and better life, he reached home a little before nine at night.

The snow of the little quadrangle in front of the house was lit up by the light in the bedroom windows of his old nurse, Agafea Mihalovna, who performed the duties of housekeeper in his house. She was not asleep yet. Kouzma, woken by her, came shuffling sleepily out onto the steps. A setter, Laska, ran out too, almost knocking Kouzma over, and, whining, circled around Levin's knees, jumping up and longing — but not daring — to put her forepaws on his chest.
"You're back soon, sir," said Agafea Mihalovna.
"I got tired of all of it, Agafea Mihalovna. With friends one is fine; at home one is better," he answered, and went into his study.

The study lit up slowly as the candle was brought in. The familiar details came out: the stag's horns, the bookshelves, the mirror, the stove with its ventilator that had long needed mending, his father's sofa, a large table, on the table an open book, a broken ashtray, a notebook in his own hand. As he saw all this, there came over him for an instant a doubt about being able to arrange the new life he had been dreaming of on the road. All these traces of his life seemed to grab at him and tell him: "No, you're not going to get away from us; you're not going to be any different; you'll go on being the same as you always have — with your doubts, your everlasting dissatisfaction with yourself, your useless attempts to amend, and your falls, and your eternal expectation of a happiness you won't get and which isn't possible for you."

These were the things telling him this, but another voice in his heart was saying that he must not fall under the sway of the past, and that one can do anything with oneself. And on hearing that voice, he went into the corner where his two heavy dumbbells stood and began swinging them like a gymnast, trying to restore his confident mood. There was a creak of steps at the door. He hastily put down the dumbbells.

The bailiff came in and said everything, thank God, was going well; but informed him that the buckwheat in the new drying machine had been a bit scorched. This piece of news irritated Levin. The new drying machine had been built and partly invented by Levin. The bailiff had always been against the drying machine, and now it was with suppressed triumph that he reported the buckwheat had been scorched. Levin was firmly convinced that if the buckwheat had been scorched it was only because the precautions had not been taken that he had given orders about hundreds of times. He was annoyed and gave the bailiff a reprimand. But there had been an important and joyful event: Pava, his best cow, an expensive beast bought at a show, had calved.
"Kouzma, get me my sheepskin. And you, tell them to bring a lantern. I'll come and have a look at her," he said to the bailiff.

The cowhouse for the more valuable cows was just behind the house. Walking across the yard, passing a snowdrift by the lilac tree, he went into the cowhouse. There was the warm, steamy smell of dung as the frozen door opened, and the cows, startled by the unfamiliar light of the lantern, stirred on the fresh straw. He caught a glimpse of the broad, smooth, black-and-piebald back of Hollandka. Berkoot, the bull, was lying down with his ring in his lip, and seemed about to get up, but thought better of it and only gave two snorts as they passed him. Pava, a perfect beauty, huge as a hippopotamus, with her back turned to them, kept them from seeing the calf as she sniffed it all over.

Levin went into the pen, looked Pava over, and lifted the red-and-spotted calf onto her long, tottering legs. Pava, uneasy, started lowing, but when Levin set the calf close to her she calmed down, and, with a heavy sigh, began licking it with her rough tongue. The calf, fumbling, poked her nose under her mother's udder and stiffened her tail out straight.

"Here, Fyodor, bring the light over this way," Levin said, looking the calf over. "She's like the mother — though the color is more like the father; but that's nothing. Very good. Long and broad in the haunch. Vassily Fedorovitch, isn't she splendid?" he said to the bailiff, completely forgiving him about the buckwheat under the spell of his delight in the calf.

"How could she fail to be, sir? Oh, Semyon the contractor came the day after you left. You'll need to settle up with him, Konstantin Dmitrievitch," the bailiff said. "I did tell you about the machine."

This one question was enough to plunge Levin back into all the details of his work on the estate, which was on a large and complicated scale. He walked straight from the cowhouse to the counting house, and after a brief talk with the bailiff and Semyon the contractor, returned to the house and went straight upstairs to the drawing-room.
